text: Gerhard Richter, born on 9 February 1932 in Dresden-Neustadt, Saxony, is a German visual artist known for his abstract and photorealistic paintings, photographs, and glass pieces. He is widely regarded as one of the most important contemporary German artists, with several of his works setting record auction prices, and he was once the most expensive living painter. Richter has been described as the "greatest living painter," "the world's most important artist," and the "Picasso of the 21st century." He grew up in Reichenau (now Bogatynia, Poland) and Waltersdorf (Zittauer Gebirge), where his father, Horst Richter, worked as a village teacher and studied mathematics and physics at the Technische Hochschule in Dresden; he married Hildegard Schönfelder in 1931. Hildegard, who was 25 when she gave birth to Gerhard, had a father, Ernst Alfred Schönfelder, once considered a gifted pianist; after moving to Dresden to take over the family brewing business, which eventually went bankrupt, the family relocated. Hildegard trained as a bookseller and developed a passion for literature and music. Horst joined the National Socialist Party after struggling in the new education system, though he remained apolitical and was not required to attend rallies. At age 10, Gerhard was conscripted into the Hitler Youth, which was dissolved before he reached enlistment age. In 1943, Hildegard moved the family to Waltersdorf and later sold her piano. Two of Hildegard’s brothers died in the war, and her sister, Gerhard’s aunt Marianne, who had schizophrenia, was starved to death in a psychiatric clinic as a victim of the Nazi euthanasia program. Richter left school after the 10th grade and apprenticed as an advertising and stage-set painter, completing vocational high school in Zittau in 1948. Between 1949 and 1951, he worked as an apprentice with a sign painter and as a painter; his application to the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts in 1950 was rejected as "too bourgeois," and he began studying there in 1951 under teachers Karl von Appen, Heinz Lohmar, and Will Grohmann. In 1957, he married Marianne Eufinger, who gave birth to his first daughter; he married sculptor Isa Genzken in 1982 and had two sons and a daughter with his third wife, Sabine Moritz, whom he married in 1995. Early in his career, he created a wall painting titled Communion with Picasso (1955) for the Academy’s refectory and a mural, Lebensfreude (Joy of Life), for the German Hygiene Museum, intended to resemble wallpaper or tapestry. From 1957 to 1961, he worked as a master trainee in the academy and took commissions for East Germany, producing murals like Arbeiterkampf (Workers' Struggle), portraits of East German actress Angelica Domröse and his first wife Ema, self-portraits, and a panorama of Dresden titled Stadtbild (Townscape, 1956). In 1961, he and his wife Marianne escaped from East to West Germany two months before the Berlin Wall was built; both of their Academy and Hygiene Museum wall paintings were later painted over for ideological reasons. After German reunification, parts of the Joy of Life mural were uncovered in the stairway of the Hygiene Museum in 2024, though they were previously covered when the museum was restored to its 1930 state. In West Germany, Richter studied at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf under Karl Otto Götz alongside Sigmar Polke, Werner Hilsing, HA Schult, Kuno Gonschior, Franz Erhard Walther, Konrad Lueg, and Gotthard Graubner. With Polke and Konrad Fischer (pseudonym Lueg), he introduced the term Kapitalistischer Realismus (Capitalistic Realism) as an anti-style of art, appropriating advertising imagery and critiquing both Socialist Realism and Western consumer-driven art. He taught at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg and the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design as a visiting professor and returned to the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in 1971, where he taught for over 15 years. In 1983, he moved to Cologne, where he still lives and works. In 1996, he moved into a studio designed by architect Thiess Marwede. During the 1960s and early 1970s, he created paintings from black-and-white photographs based on newspapers, books, private snapshots, aerial views of towns and mountains (e.g., Cityscape Madrid (1968) and Alps (1968)), seascapes (1969–70), and a large multipart work for the German Pavilion at the 1972 Venice Biennale. For Forty-eight Portraits (1971–72), he painted faces of composers like Gustav Mahler and Jean Sibelius and writers like H. G. Wells and Franz Kafka. From around 1964, he made portraits of dealers, collectors, and artists; his two portraits of his daughter Betty were made in 1977 and 1988, and three portraits titled IG from 1993 depict his second wife, Isa Genzken. Lesende (1994) portrays Sabine Moritz, shown reading a magazine. Many of his realist paintings reflect on Nazi history, depicting family members who were members or victims of the regime. From 1966, he began using photographs he took himself as the basis for portraits. In 1975, on the occasion of a Düsseldorf show, Gilbert & George commissioned a portrait from him. Richter began making prints in 1965, producing over 100 works between 1965 and 1974, using screenprint, photolithography, and collotype to achieve a "non-art" appearance; he stopped print work in 1974 and began painting from photographs he took. Early landscape elements appeared in 1963, but he began an independent series in 1968 after a vacation in Corsica. His landscapes are compared to Caspar David Friedrich and are understood within the context of traditional German Romantic Painting. Große Teyde-Landschaft (1971) draws from holiday snapshots of Tenerife. Atlas, first exhibited in 1972 at the Museum voor Hedendaagse Kunst in Utrecht under the title Atlas der Fotos und Skizzen, included 315 parts and has continued to expand, being fully exhibited at the Lenbachhaus in Munich in 1989, the Museum Ludwig in Cologne in 1990, and the Dia Art Foundation in New York in 1995. Atlas remains an ongoing, encyclopedic work composed of approximately 4,000 photographs, reproductions, or cut-out details on about 600 panels. In 1972, Richter made a ten-day trip to Greenland alone, intending to record the arctic landscape; in 1976, four large paintings titled Seascape emerged from these photographs. In 1982 and 1983, he created a series of paintings of Candles and Skulls, inspired by vanitas painters like Georges de La Tour and Francisco de Zurbarán, based on studio photographs, arranged in varying natural light on barren tables. He made only 27 of these still lifes; in 1995, he created a monumental solitary candle over the River Elbe to mark the 50th anniversary of the Allied bombings of Dresden. Richter described the series as evoking feelings of contemplation, memory, silence, and death. In 1988, he produced a series of 15 ambiguous photo paintings entitled 18 October 1977, depicting members of the Red Army Faction (RAF), based on black-and-white newspaper and police photos. The paintings were created from official portraits of Ulrike Meinhof, photos of Holger Meins’ arrest, police shots of Gudrun Ensslin in prison, Andreas Baader’s bookshelves and record player, and images of the dead RAF members and Ensslin’s funeral. Since 1989, he has created new images by dragging wet paint over photographs, mostly snapshots of daily life such as family vacations, friends, mountains, buildings, and streetscapes. In 2001, Richter was flying to New York on 11 September but was diverted to Halifax due to the 9/11 attacks; a few years later, he made a small painting about the planes crashing into the World Trade Center. Robert Storr, in his 2005 analysis of Richter’s painting September, situates it within an anti-ideological framework and compares it to the 18 October 1977 series regarding photographic documentation and memory. In the 2000s, Richter created works on scientific phenomena; in 2003, he produced several paintings titled Silicate, large oil-on-canvas pieces showing latticed rows of light- and dark-grey blobs that quasi-repeat and shift in angle, based on a photo from the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung of computer-generated reflections from silicon dioxide in insects’ shells. In 2014, he created a cycle of four paintings titled Birkenau using Sonderkommando photographs from Auschwitz-Birkenau, which were made permanently available to the International Auschwitz Committee in October 2021 and are on permanent display in a pavilion on the grounds of the International Youth Meeting Center in Oświęcim/Auschwitz, about 2 kilometers from the Auschwitz II-Birkenau site, designed by Richter. In 2024, an edition of the Birkenau works as prints on metal plate, made and donated by Richter, went on display at the Centre. His early work Table (1962) was a painting of a table from a magazine photograph with tachiste gestural marks overlapping, using haptic swirls of grey paint to cancel the photorealist image and introduce generativity. In 1969, he produced the first of a group of grey monochromes made exclusively from textures from different paint application methods. In 1976, he first titled a work Abstract Painting, stating that by naming it without explanation, he was "letting a thing come, rather than creating it." His abstract paintings build up layers of non-representational paint, beginning with large swaths of primary color, evolving through spontaneous, reactive gestures, and using techniques like blurring and scraping to veil and expose prior layers. From the mid-1980s, he began using a homemade squeegee to rub and scrape paint applied in large bands; in interviews, he linked his grey and abstract works to artists like Bob Ryman, Brice Marden, Alan Charlton, and Yves Klein. In the 1990s, he began running his squeegee up and down the canvas to create vertical columns resembling a wall of planks. His abstract work, though lacking natural palettes and space, often appears as a window to an external landscape, equalizing illusion and paint, reducing worldly images to art incidents, and elevating intuitive mark-making to spatial believability. Firenze is a cycle of 99 works conceived in autumn 1999 and executed in that year and afterward, part of the overpainted photographs (übermalte Fotographien) series, which includes over 2,000 pieces; it consists of small paintings of Florence created as a tribute to Steve Reich and the Contempoartensemble. After 2000, Richter made works on scientific phenomena, particularly those invisible to the naked eye, including in 2006.

Despite unnatural palettes, spaceless sheets of color, and visible trails of the artist's tools, Gerhard Richter's abstract paintings often function like windows, allowing viewers to perceive an external landscape. This effect parallels his representational works, where worldly images are reduced to mere incidents of art; similarly, in his abstract pieces, Richter elevates spontaneous, intuitive mark-making to a level of spatial logic and believability. Firenze is a series of 99 small paintings created in the autumn of 1999 and executed in that year and beyond, depicting the city of Florence as a tribute to Steve Reich and the Contempoartensemble, a Florence-based musical group. This series belongs to the broader body of overpainted photographs, or übermalte Fotographien, which includes more than 2,000 works. After 2000, Richter produced works exploring scientific phenomena, particularly those invisible to the naked eye. In 2006, he created six paintings titled Cage, named after American avant-garde composer John Cage, using large canvases with intersecting fields, lines, and uneven smears generated by dragging a squeegee tool and removing paint to reveal layered patches. In May 2002, Richter photographed 216 details from his abstract painting no. 648-2 (1987), 10 x 15 cm in size, and combined them with 165 texts from the German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (published on 20 and 21 March) to produce a 2004 book titled War Cut. In November 2008, Richter began a series applying ink droplets to wet paper, using alcohol and lacquer to control ink bloom and creep, resulting in double-sided works; sometimes upper sheets bled into others, forming sequential images, and in some cases, lacquer was applied or pencil lines were drawn across color patches. As early as 1966, Richter created paintings based on color charts, drawing inspiration from found objects that arranged colored rectangles in limitless hues. His experiments culminated in 1973–74 with large-format works such as 256 Colours, and between 1966 and 1974, he produced three series of Color Chart works, each growing more ambitious in its attempt to generate meaning through arbitrary color arrangements. His first series began with a small painting entitled 10 Colors, where he used his friend Blinky Palermo to randomly call out colors. In the 1970s, Richter shifted focus from readymade objects to conceptual systems, using mathematical procedures for mixing primary colors in graduated amounts and random ordering to determine color placement. His second series of Color Charts consisted of five paintings, and the final series from 1973–1974 introduced light grey, dark grey, and later green into the permutational system. Richter's 4900 Colours from 2007 features bright monochrome squares randomly arranged in a grid, forming kaleidoscopic fields; it consists of 196 panels in 25 colors, reassembled in 11 variations, including a version with 49 paintings measuring 97 by 97 centimeters, developed specifically for the Serpentine Gallery. Richter began using glass in 1967 with Four Panes of Glass, which could tilt at varying angles. In 1970, he and Blinky Palermo jointly proposed a design for the 1972 Munich Olympic arena featuring 27 different colored glass windows, each appearing fifty times, distributed randomly. In 1981, for a two-person show with Georg Baselitz in Düsseldorf, Richter created the first of his monumental transparent mirrors, larger than his paintings and featuring adjustable steel mounts; for example, Mirror Painting (Grey, 735-2) (1991) used grey pigment on the glass's back. At Documenta 9 in Kassel in 1992, Richter presented a pavilion with paintings and colored mirrors designed in collaboration with architect Paul Robbrecht. In 2002, for the Dia Art Foundation, Richter created a glass sculpture including Spiegel I and Spiegel II (1989), measuring 7 feet tall and 18 feet long, which alters the gallery environment and visual experience, and Kugel (Sphere) (1992), a stainless steel mirror reflecting space. Since 2002, he has produced three-dimensional glass constructions such as 6 Standing Glass Panels (2002/2011). In 2010, the Drawing Center presented Lines which do not exist, a survey of Richter's drawings from 1966 to 2005, including works made with mechanical intervention like a pencil attached to an electric hand drill; it was the first U.S. career overview since the 2002 MoMA retrospective. R. H. Lossin wrote in The Brooklyn Rail that Richter's drawing practice documented a hand that couldn't draw properly, displacing the artist's hand with material evidence of failure. Throughout his career, Richter has declined lucrative licensing deals and private commissions. Domplatz, Mailand (1968), a 9 by 9.5-foot painting depicting the Milan Duomo and Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, was a Siemens commission that hung in the company's Milan offices from 1968 to 1998; it was sold by Sotheby's in London in 1998 for $3.6 million. In 1980, Richter and Isa Genzken were commissioned to design the König-Heinrich-Platz underground station in Duisburg, completed in 1992. In 1986, he received commissions for two large-scale paintings, Victoria I and Victoria II, from the Victoria insurance company in Düsseldorf. In 1990, he co-created works for the Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechselbank in Düsseldorf with Sol LeWitt and Oswald Mathias Ungers. In 1998, he installed a wall piece based on Germany's flag in the rebuilt Reichstag in Berlin. In 2012, he designed the first page of the German newspaper Die Welt. In 2017, he designed the label for the 2015 Chateau Mouton Rothschild's first wine. In 2002, Richter was commissioned to design a stained glass window for the Cologne Cathedral, unveiled in August 2007; it covers 113 square meters (1,220 sq ft), consists of 11,500 pixel-like squares in 72 colors arranged randomly by computer (with some symmetry), reminiscent of his 1974 painting 4096 Colours, and was created without fee, with costs of around €370,000 ($506,000) covered by donations from over 1,000 people. Cardinal Joachim Meisner did not attend the unveiling, preferring a figurative depiction of 20th-century Christian martyrs, and stated the window would fit better in a mosque or prayer house; Richter, a professed atheist with a strong leaning toward Catholicism, had his three children baptized in the Cologne Cathedral. In September 2020, Richter unveiled three 30-foot-tall stained-glass windows for Tholey Abbey, one of Germany's oldest monasteries, which he called his last major work, after which he would focus on drawings and sketches. The windows were made by Gustva van Treeck in Munich and are abstract painted works inspired by his "Pattern" series from the 1990s. An additional 34 figurative stained-glass windows by Afghan-German Muslim artist Mahbuba Maqsoodi are expected to be completed by Easter 2021. The monks hoped the windows would promote tourism and bring people into faith. Richter first exhibited in Düsseldorf in 1963 and had his first gallery solo show in 1964 at Galerie Schmela in Düsseldorf. Soon after, he exhibited in Munich and Berlin, and by the early 1970s, he exhibited frequently throughout Europe and the United States. In 1966, Bruno Bischofberger was the first to show Richter's works outside Germany. His first retrospective was at the Kunsthalle Bremen in 1976, covering works from 1962 to 1974. A traveling retrospective at Düsseldorf's Kunsthalle in 1986 was followed in 1991 by a retrospective at the Tate Gallery, London. In 1993, he received a major touring retrospective "Gerhard Richter: Malerei 1962–1993" curated by Kasper König, with a three-volume catalogue edited by Benjamin Buchloh, which entirely reinvented his career. Richter gained recognition in the U.S. in 1990 with the Saint Louis Art Museum's show of Baader-Meinhof (18 October 1977), later seen at the Lannan Foundation in Marina del Rey. His first North American retrospective was in 1998 at the Art Gallery of Ontario and the Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago. In 2002, a 40-year retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, traveled to the Art Institute of Chicago, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Washington, D.C. In 2016, he participated in the international exhibition Doppelgänger, curated by Sandra Mann, Ichiro Irie, Julia-Constance Dissel, Max Presneill, at the Torrance Art Museum, California. His work is included in permanent collections in the U.S., such as the Pérez Art Museum Miami. He has participated in several international art shows, including the Venice Biennale (1972, 1980, 1984, 1997, 2007) and Documenta V (1972), VII (1982), VIII (1987), IX (1992), and X (1997). In 2006, a Getty Center exhibition linked Richter's landscapes to Caspar David Friedrich's Romantic works, noting both artists used abstraction, expansiveness, and emptiness to express transcendent emotion. The Gerhard Richter Archive was established in 2005 in cooperation with the artist as an institute of the Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden. In 2020, Gerhard Richter established the Gerhard Richter Art Foundation, a non-profit dedicated to preserving his work and making it available for exhibitions. The first major exhibition of his work in Australia, Gerhard Richter: The Life of Images, was held by the Queensland Gallery of Modern Art in Brisbane from 14 October 2017 to 4 February 2018, including over 90 works, such as the newly created Atlas Overview, a 400-panel extract selected by Richter from the larger Atlas project now deemed too fragile for travel. In 2022, the Raphael Durazzo Gallery exhibited 2014: 20. November 2014, oil on colored photograph, 15 x 10 cm. Richter gained widespread fame during his 2005 retrospective, which declared his status as one of the most important artists of the 20th century, and today many consider him the best living painter. This reputation stems in part from his ability to explore painting during a time when many believed its medium was dying. He has received numerous awards, including the State Prize of North Rhine-Westphalia (2000), the Wexner Prize (1998), the Praemium Imperiale (Japan, 1997), the Golden Lion at the 47th Venice Biennale (1997), the Wolf Prize (Israel, 1994/5), the Goslarer Kaiserring Prize (1988), the Oskar Kokoschka Prize (Vienna, 1985), the Arnold Bode Prize (Kassel, 1981), and the Junger Western Art Prize (Germany, 1961). He was made an honorary citizen of Cologne in April 2007 and elected to the American Philosophical Society in 2012. Among his students at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf between 1971 and 1994 were Ludger Gerdes, Hans-Jörg Holubitschka, Bernard Lokai, Thomas Schütte, Thomas Struth, Katrin Kneffel, Michael van Ofen, and his second wife, Isa Genzken. He influenced Ellsworth Kelly, Christopher Wool, and Johan Andersson. He has also inspired writers and musicians; Sonic Youth used a painting of his for the cover of their 1988 album Daydream Nation, and he did not charge for the use of the image; the original, over 7 meters (23 feet) square, is now displayed in Sonic Youth's studio in NYC. Don DeLillo's short story "Baader-Meinhof" describes a meeting between two strangers at the MoMA in the room displaying 18 October 1977 (1988). Photographer Cotton Coulson described Richter as one of his favorite artists. For the last 18 years, Richter has ranked number one on a Kunstkompass scale of the most important world artists, made by German magazine Capital. Following an exhibition with Blinky Palermo at Galerie Heiner Friedrich in 1971, Richter ended his formal arrangement with the dealer in 1972; thereafter, Friedrich could only sell paintings he had already obtained under contract. Don DeLillo's short story "Baader-Meinhof" features an encounter between two strangers at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, taking place in the room displaying 18 October 1977 (1988). Photographer Cotton Coulson described Gerhard Richter as "one of [his] favourite artists". For the last 18 years, Richter has ranked number one on a Kunstkompass scale of most important world artists, compiled by the German magazine Capital. Following an exhibition with Blinky Palermo at Galerie Heiner Friedrich in 1971, Richter's formal arrangement with the dealer ended in 1972, after which Friedrich could only sell paintings he had already obtained contractually. In subsequent years, Richter exhibited at Galerie Konrad Fischer in Düsseldorf and Sperone Westwater in New York. From 1985 to 2022, his primary dealer and representative gallery was Marian Goodman; since December 2022, he has been represented by David Zwirner Gallery. Today, museums own roughly 38% of Richter's works, including half of his large abstract paintings. By 2004, Richter's annual turnover reached $120 million. According to artnet, $76.9 million worth of Richter's work was sold at auction in 2010. As of 2012, at least 545 distinct Richter works had sold at auctions for over $100,000, with 15 selling for more than $10,000,000 between 2007 and 2012. Richter's paintings have been steadily moving out of Germany since the mid-1990s, although certain key German collectors—Frieder Burda, Josef Fröhlich, Georg Böckmann, and Ulrich Ströher—have retained their holdings. Richter's candle paintings were the first to achieve high auction prices; three months after his MoMA exhibition opened in 2001, Sotheby's sold his Three Candles (1982) for $5.3 million. In February 2008, his eldest daughter, Betty, sold her Kerze (1983) for £7,972,500 ($15 million), triple the high estimate, at Sotheby's in London. His 1982 Kerze sold for £10.5 million ($16.5 million) at Christie's London in October 2011. In February 2008, Christie's London set a record for Richter's "capitalist realism" works from the 1960s by selling Zwei Liebespaare (1966) for £7,300,500 ($14.3 million) to Stephan Schmidheiny. In 2010, the Weserburg modern art museum in Bremen sold Richter's 1966 Matrosen (Sailors) at a Sotheby's auction in November, where John D. Arnold bought it for $13 million. Vierwaldstätter See, one of four views of Lake Lucerne painted by Richter in 1969, sold for £15.8 million ($24 million) at Christie's London in 2015. Another highly sought group is the Abstrakte Bilder series, especially those made after 1988, finished with a large squeegee rather than a brush or roller. At Pierre Bergé & Associés in July 2009, Richter's 1979 oil painting Abstraktes Bild sold for €95,000 ($136,000), exceeding its estimate. Richter's 1990 Abstraktes Bild achieved a record price of 7.2 million pounds, or about $11.6 million, at a Sotheby's sale in February 2011, attributed to a bidder believed to be an agent for New York dealer Larry Gagosian. In November 2011, Sotheby's sold a group of colorful abstract canvases by Richter, including Abstraktes Bild 849-3, which set a record price for the artist when Lily Safra paid $20.8 million and later donated it to the Israel Museum. Months later, Christie's sold the 1993 painting Abstraktes Bild 798-3 for a record $21.8 million. Abstraktes Bild (809–4), an abstract canvas from 1994, was sold by Eric Clapton at Sotheby's in late 2012 for $34.2 million, estimated to bring $14.1 million to $18.8 million. This was surpassed in May 2013 when his 1968 Cathedral Square, Milan sold for $37.1 million (£24.4 million) in New York. In February 2015, his 1986 painting Abstraktes Bild (599) sold for $44.52 million (£30.4 million) at Sotheby's Contemporary Evening Sale in London, becoming the highest price at auction for contemporary art at the time; this record was later broken on 12 November 2013 when Jeff Koons' Balloon Dog (Orange) sold for US$58.4 million at Christie's in New York. When asked about such prices, Richter remarked, "It's just as absurd as the banking crisis. It's impossible to understand and it's daft!" In 2003, Gerald Fox produced a documentary on Richter's life. In 2007, Corinna Belz made a short film titled Gerhard Richter's Window. In 2011, Belz released a feature-length documentary, Gerhard Richter Painting, focusing on the world's highest-paid living artist creating large-scale abstract squeegee works in his studio. The 2018 drama film Never Look Away is inspired by Richter's life story. In 2016 and 2019, Richter collaborated with Corinna Belz on two films based on his 2012 book Patterns. The first, Richters Patterns, when shown, is paired with music by German composer Marcus Schmickler, and the later one with music by American composer Steve Reich, both performed by a live ensemble. The latter work is part of a larger two-section collaboration, Reich Richter Pärt, commissioned for the inaugural season at The Shed in the Hudson Yards development in Manhattan, New York City.
